title: Turn on two-factor login

cards.text: Two-factor login adds a second step when you log in. It can be a code texted to your phone. CISA says that even if a password is stolen, a person without the second step can't get in.
cards.line: Your password is the first step. This adds a second one.

cards.text: Never read a code to someone who contacts you first. The FTC says some people try to trick you into giving them the code.
Two-factor login is not usually on by default. To turn it on, open the account's settings and look for two-factor or two-step. Some sites call it multi-factor.
cards.line: Start with your most sensitive accounts, like your email and your bank.

checks.prompt: Which account should get two-factor login first?
options: A shopping site you used once
checks.why: The FTC says to start with your most sensitive accounts. Your email and bank are a good start.

checks.prompt: A caller asks for the code that was just texted to you. Which is the safer step?
options: Read it to them if they sound real
Text it to them right away
checks.why: The FTC says not to share it if you didn't contact them first.

checks.prompt: You want to turn on two-factor login for your email. Where do you start?
options: Wait for the site to turn it on
checks.why: It's not usually on by default. The FTC says to go to your account settings and look for two-factor or two-step.

takeaway: Start with your email and your bank.

sources.name: CISA, Protect Our World with MFA
